title: Improving Language Understanding by Generative Pre-Training (GPT-1)
authors: Alec Radford, Karthik Narasimhan, Tim Salimans, Ilya Sutskever

pages.title: Pre-train a Transformer LM, fine-tune on downstream tasks

blocks.html: Before this paper, NLP models were typically trained task-by-task from scratch, sometimes initialized with word embeddings (word2vec, GloVe). Labeled data is expensive; unlabeled text is abundant. The motivating question: can we use the unlabeled text to do most of the learning, and adapt cheaply?

items: Step 1 — pre-train a Transformer decoder on a large unlabeled corpus (BooksCorpus, 7000 books, ~800M words) with a standard left-to-right language modeling objective.
Step 2 — fine-tune the pre-trained model on each downstream task, with a small task-specific input transformation and an extra linear layer. Whole model is updated.

blocks.html: This is the recipe that the entire pre-train-then-fine-tune era runs on. GPT-1 was the first paper to show it could be applied uniformly across a range of NLP tasks and beat task-specific models on most of them.

$\mathcal{U}$ is the unlabeled token corpus, $k$ is the context window. The model: a 12-layer Transformer decoder (the masked self-attention variant), 12 heads, hidden size 768, FFN size 3072. ~117M parameters.
BPE tokenization with 40k merges. Position embeddings are learned (not sinusoidal). Trained for 100 epochs on BooksCorpus, ~8 GPU-days on 8 P600 GPUs.
Given labeled examples $(x^1, \ldots, x^m, y)$, feed the inputs through the pre-trained Transformer, take the final hidden state of the last token, push through a linear classifier:

Auxiliary LM loss: also keep the language modeling loss active during fine-tuning, weighted by a small $\lambda$. This serves as a regularizer and prevents catastrophic forgetting of pre-trained knowledge.
Different NLP tasks have different input structures. Rather than design a different architecture per task, GPT-1 flattens every task into a single sequence with delimiter tokens:

items: Similarity: two orderings [start] A [delim] B [extract] and [start] B [delim] A [extract]; sum the final reps.
Multiple choice: [start] context [delim] choice_i [extract] for each choice; softmax over the resulting logits.

blocks.html: This 'turn everything into language' framing is the template GPT-2, GPT-3, and modern chat models all follow.
Improved state-of-the-art on 9 of 12 evaluated tasks at release:

items: Natural language inference: SNLI, MNLI, QNLI, RTE — all improved.
Question answering: RACE, Story Cloze — large gains.
Classification: SST-2 — at state of the art.

blocks.html: Crucially, the same pre-trained model is the starting point for all of them. Earlier work needed bespoke architectures and ad-hoc word embeddings; GPT-1 needed one model and a different last layer.

items: Pre-training is essential — without it, the same architecture trained from scratch performs much worse.
Number of pre-training layers transferred matters — performance improves nearly monotonically as you transfer more layers.
The auxiliary LM loss helps on larger datasets, mildly hurts on smaller ones.
A Transformer base beats a comparable LSTM base by ~5 absolute on average — the architecture matters too, not just pre-training.

blocks.html: GPT-1 introduced the recipe that, scaled up, became GPT-2 (1.5B params, 2019), GPT-3 (175B, 2020), GPT-4 (2023), and the entire modern LLM industry. The architectural choice (decoder-only autoregressive Transformer) and the methodology (pre-train on a huge unlabeled corpus, adapt to downstream tasks) both come straight from this paper.

BERT (released a few months later) took the same idea in a different direction (bidirectional masked LM). Both papers became foundational; both pre-training recipes are now part of standard ML curriculum.
